lines.text: On a September afternoon in nineteen forty-seven, a computer was stopped by an insect.
Not a figure of speech. A moth.
Its body is still taped to a page in a logbook, in a museum in Washington.
Beside it, one line of handwriting.
First actual case of bug being found.
This is the story of the Harvard Mark Two.
And of a word every programmer uses, every single day.
And almost everyone tells it wrong.
Harvard University. Cambridge, Massachusetts.
The Mark Two was built to crunch numbers for the United States Navy.
It filled a room.
No screen. No keyboard. No silicon.
Instead, thousands of relays.
Tiny metal switches, snapping open and shut with every calculation.
The operators worked in shifts, keeping a logbook of every run.
Every test. Every failure. Every fix.
But on the ninth of September, something went wrong.
The machine kept giving errors.
The team went looking, panel by panel, relay by relay.
At three forty-five in the afternoon, they found it.
Panel F. Relay number seventy.
A moth, crushed between the contacts.
It had stopped the switch from closing.
Someone pulled it out with tweezers, and taped it into the log.
Then wrote the line underneath.
But here is the twist.
Engineers were already calling faults bugs.
Thomas Edison used the word in letters back in the eighteen seventies.
So the operators were not naming anything.
They were making a pun.
For once, the bug was an actual bug.
The story spread through Grace Hopper, a Navy officer and programmer on the team.
She told it for decades, in talks around the world.
Many still believe she found the moth, or invented the word.
She did neither.
But she made sure nobody forgot it.
The logbook reached the Smithsonian in nineteen ninety-four.
The moth is still there, flat and brown, almost eighty years later.
Every crash, every glitch, every patch since then carries its name.
Machines don't fail in grand ways.
They fail in tiny places nobody thought to look.
